HGIS Lab · homestead register transcription · sampling plan

Where to Transcribe Next

The registers cover 3,455 townships. 882 are fully typed and dated — a purposive sample built around the Saskatoon–Battleford–Prince Albert–Batoche zone, the Qu'Appelle valley, the CPR belt, and a few others. This page measures how that sample differs from the province on things we can know for every township without transcribing it, and proposes an order of work that turns it into a defensible sample of the whole.

Where the work stands

A township counts as done when at least half its quarter-section rows carry a Type; in practice done townships are 90–100% typed and the rest are under 1%, so the cut is unambiguous. Names only townships (1,904) carry names scraped from the Provincial Archives' homestead index — one per homestead file on the quarter — but no register transcription yet: no type, no dates, no sales or railway/HBC/school quarters, and no homestead-vs-pre-emption distinction. Empty townships (669) have no index file on more than 70% of their quarters — forest reserve, lake, ranch-lease and reserve country, mostly north of T48 and around the Cypress Hills.

The era proxy is the earliest of: a railway built within 16 km of the township centre (rail_lines.geojson), a 1921 incorporated town founded within 25 km (townsites.geojson), or a grain elevator licensed within 15 km (stations.geojson). It is not the settlement date — the registers will give that — but it is known for every township, which is what a sampling frame needs. The right-hand map shows the problem at a glance: the solid (done) townships sit almost entirely in the dark-blue early-settled core, while the pale 1906+ and grey remote townships are faded out.

The index layer is itself a province-wide covariate

Because the scraped index exists for every township, it gives two things the register transcription cannot yet: the density of homestead files (which quarters ever had a homestead entry) and a churn signal — a quarter with two or more names had at least one entry cancelled or abandoned before the last. Province-wide the index has files on 282,022 quarter sections; 97,827 (34.7%) carry two or more names and 31,859 (11.3%) three or more.

Calibration. Eight sheets (W2 R13, R15–R17; W3 R11, R17–R19) were index-only in June and transcribed by August, so the two layers can be compared on the same 8,013 quarters. The index flags 40.1% of them as multi-name, the register 50.1%; they agree on 79% of quarters, and the register finds more names (mean 1.74 vs 1.59) — cancelled entries that never produced an index line. So the index reads roughly ten points low but tracks the register. It has a file for 95% of the quarters the register types as homestead or pre-emption and for almost none of the railway, HBC, school-land or reserve quarters: a near-complete inventory of homestead-type land and nothing else, which is why the register pass is needed.

Churn climbs with settlement era — 31% of files in pre-1890 townships, 33% in 1901–05, 41.5% in 1906–10, 46% in townships settled after 1910 — and is highest in the dry south (38%), in W3 (37%) and outside the CPR belt (37% against 28% inside). On the register's own measure the done townships show 49.2% multi-name on homestead and pre-emption quarters — an index-equivalent of about 39% after calibration, close to the 40.0% the index shows for the townships not yet done. So the sample is not badly off on churn overall; what it lacks is the high-churn end of the gradient, the 1906+ dry south and fringe, where the index says failure ran to 42–46% before the register's extra cancellations are counted. Those are zones A, B and C.

Values in brown are below 70% of the provincial rate (26%). Read together: the sample over-weights the 1880s CPR corridor and the parkland, the two zones that were chosen first, and under-weights the late-settled dry south-west, the forest fringe, the remote north, and every township without CPR land. For the liberal-order questions that matters directly — the 1908–12 pre-emption belt, the soldier-settlement and 1920s fringe, and the non-railway townships are exactly the cases where free land, priced land and failure behaved differently.

Of the 30 era × band cells, 7 currently have no done township at all (every 1911+ cell outside the parkland, and the 1890s and 1901–05 forest fringe). Any provincial estimate built by post-stratifying the existing data is undefined for those cells.

Recommendation

1. Lay down the spine first

Transcribe (Type + dates) every township where range ≡ 1 (mod 3) and township ≡ 1 (mod 3) — ranges 1, 4, 7, 10 … and townships 1, 4, 7, 10 … — in every meridian, skipping the ones already done. That is a 1-in-9 systematic spatial sample: 289 townships, 40,394 rows. At the June–August pace (~24,000 typed rows a month) it is about 1.7 months of work.

Why this rather than more zones: a systematic grid is a probability sample of the province, so estimates from it (settlement year, failure rate, tenure mix, entry-to-patent lag) carry standard errors and can be reported as provincial figures. It also reaches every stratum at once. After the spine, 1911+ coverage rises from 4% to 15%, the forest fringe from 11% to 22%, non-CPR townships from 18% to 28%, and the empty era × band cells fall from 7 to 1. The offset (1, 1) was chosen among the nine possible because it lands most evenly across eras.

Practical shape of the spine. Sheets are ranges, so the spine touches every third sheet: R01, R04, R07, R10, R13, R16, R19, R22, R25, R28 in W2 and W3, plus R31, R34 in W1. Within each, type the rows for townships 1, 4, 7, … 55 (nine to nineteen townships a sheet). Because the CPR odd sections are typed in the same pass, each township is ~144 rows.

2. Then infill by zone, in this order

The spine leaves the sample thin where the frame is largest. These zones are ranked by how under-represented their townships are (mean weight of the era × band × meridian cell); the spine townships inside each are already counted in step 1.

  • A and B — the dry south-west — are the biggest single gap: 604 townships, 17 done, covering the 1908–12 pre-emption rush and the ranching-to-wheat conversion. B is the block of index-only sheets (W3 R20–R30), with some of the highest index churn in the province.
  • C — the forest fringe (T49–56) is where soldier settlement, the 1920s land rush and the 1930s relief homesteads live; half its townships have no rail, town or elevator proxy at all, which is itself the finding.
  • D — east-central parkland (Kamsack–Preeceville–Hudson Bay) is the one early-settled region with almost no coverage, and it is Doukhobor and Ukrainian block-settlement country.
  • F, E and G are smaller corrections; G (Kindersley–Kerrobert) is index-only and could be folded into the B pass.

3. What to stop doing for now

W1 is 50% covered and the CPR belt 53%; the parkland T37–48 is 35%. Further work there adds precision to strata that are already the best-known and pushes the sample further from the province. If a team member is mid-sheet in one of those areas, finishing the sheet is fine; starting a new one is not the best use of the hours.

4. Use the frame now

Even before the spine is done, provincial figures can be reported by post-stratification: weight each done township by (frame share ÷ done share) of its era × band × meridian cell. scripts/analysis/coverage_priority.py writes those weights (priority_w, and the underlying cell counts) to township_frame_scored.parquet. The 7 empty cells cannot be weighted and should be reported as "not yet sampled" until the spine fills them.

Caveats

The era proxy is infrastructure, not settlement. It leads actual homestead entry by a few years in the 1880s CPR corridor and lags it elsewhere (60% of entries preceded rail). It is used only to stratify, not to date anything.

"Done" is by township, from the Type column. A township typed but with many missing dates still counts as done; a partially typed township (there are only 17 between 1% and 90%) is not.

The spine is a design, not a guarantee. If some sheets prove much slower (poor scans, misaligned columns), swapping a spine township for its neighbour (T+1) keeps the design intact; skipping whole ranges does not.

The index churn signal is a floor. It undercounts cancellations by about ten points relative to the register (more in early-settled townships) and cannot tell a homestead from its pre-emption pair; it is used here to characterise strata, not as a substitute for transcription.

Throughput is the June 24 → Aug 25 typed-row delta (72,162 → 122,204); winter pace will differ.

Built from the W1–W3 registers (25 Aug 2026), rail_lines, townsites, stations, reserves_initial and the CPR catalogue, via scripts/analysis/coverage_frame.py → index_names.py → coverage_priority.py → coverage_report_data.py. Companion analysis: docs/analysis/register_to_freehold.html.
